lessons.title: Introduction to Casting: Sand Casting and Lost Wax
lessons.body: Casting is a 6000-year-old method for shaping metal by pouring it molten into a hollow mold. In sand casting, you pack a special sand mixture around a pattern (a replica of your sculpture), remove the pattern, and pour metal into the empty space. The sand is mixed with clay and water to hold its shape. A typical mix is 90% silica sand, 8% bentonite clay, and 2% water. For a small aluminum sculpture, you can use a two-part flask (cope and drag) made from wooden boxes. Lost wax casting is older and better for fine detail. You carve the sculpture in wax, encase it in a plaster-like ceramic shell, then heat it so the wax melts out (lost). Molten metal replaces the wax. In Africa, lost wax is famous in Benin City, Nigeria, where brass casters have used it since the 13th century. For your first project, sand casting is cheaper and faster. You can build a flask from scrap wood, and use a bucket of foundry sand. Lost wax needs more materials: microcrystalline wax, ceramic slurry, and a kiln for burnout. But lost wax gives you undercuts and thin sections. Start with sand casting for simple shapes like medallions or small figures. Both methods require safety gear: leather gloves, face shield, and a leather apron. Never pour metal over concreteâit can explode from moisture. Use a dry sand bed or steel plate.

lessons.title: Pattern Making and Mold Preparation
lessons.body: A pattern is a copy of your sculpture, but slightly larger to allow for metal shrinkage. Aluminum shrinks about 1.3% when it cools, so if you want a final piece 10 cm long, make the pattern 10.13 cm. Patterns can be made from wood, plastic, or metal. For simple shapes, carve a pattern from medium-density fiberboard (MDF) or pine. Sand the pattern smooth and apply a coat of shellac to seal it. You need a draft angleâtaper the sides by 1 to 2 degrees so you can pull the pattern out without breaking the sand. For a two-part mold, you need a parting line. Place the pattern on a flat board, then pack sand around it in the drag (bottom flask). Flip it over, place the cope (top flask), and pack more sand. Before packing, dust the pattern with talcum powder or parting dust so sand doesn't stick. Ram the sand firmly with a malletâtoo loose and the mold collapses; too hard and gases can't escape. After packing, remove the pattern by tapping it gently and lifting straight up. Cut a sprue hole (for pouring) and a riser (for gas escape) with a dowel. For lost wax, you dip the wax tree in ceramic slurry and stucco (fine sand) repeatedlyâ7 to 10 coats, drying between each. Then you melt out the wax in a kiln at 150Â°C, then fire the shell at 700Â°C. In Africa, many foundries use local clay mixed with cow dung for mold makingâit works if you test it first.

lessons.title: Melting and Pouring Metal
lessons.body: Aluminum is the easiest metal to melt for sculpture. It melts at 660Â°C. You can use a charcoal furnace made from a 20-litre metal bucket lined with clay and sand. Use charcoal or coke as fuel, and a blower (hair dryer or hand-cranked fan) to force air into the fire. A crucibleâa clay-graphite cupâholds the metal. Never use a steel pot; it will melt. Put scrap aluminum (old car rims, window frames, cans) into the crucible. Cans are too thin and oxidize; better to use cast aluminum scrap. Heat until the metal is fully liquid and shiny like mercury. Skim off dross (impurities) with a steel spoon. Pouring is the most dangerous step. Wear a face shield, leather gloves, and a leather apron. Preheat your mold to 200â300Â°C to remove moistureâif you pour into a cold mold, steam can explode molten metal back at you. Pour in one steady stream, keeping the crucible close to the sprue. Don't stop halfway. After pouring, wait until the metal turns from red to gray (about 10â15 minutes for a small casting). Then break the sand mold away with a hammer. For lost wax, quench the shell in water after it coolsâthe ceramic shatters off. In Africa, many artisans melt aluminum in small charcoal furnaces in open-air workshops. Always work outdoors or in a well-ventilated shed. Never pour near water, concrete, or flammable materials.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Finishing Castings
lessons.body: After the casting cools, you need to remove the sprue, riser, and any sand or ceramic stuck to the surface. Use a hacksaw or angle grinder with a cutting disc to cut off the sprue. Then grind the stubs flush with a grinding wheel or flap disc. For detailed areas, use a rotary tool (Dremel) with a carbide burr. Sand the surface progressively: 80 grit, then 120, 220, 400, and 800 if you want a polished finish. For a matte finish, stop at 220. Aluminum casts often have small pits and porosity. You can fill these with epoxy mixed with aluminum powder, or weld them with a TIG welder if you have one. For lost wax castings, the surface is usually smoother, but you may need to chase fine details with a graver. After sanding, clean the piece with a wire brush and soapy water. If you want a patina, you can heat the metal and apply wax or oil, or use chemical patinas like liver of sulfur (for darker tones) or ferric nitrate (for brown). In Africa, many sculptors use local materials: palm oil heated on the fire gives a rich black finish. Or bury the casting in wet ash for a weekâit darkens naturally. Always wear a dust mask when sanding or grinding, and safety glasses. Finally, sign your work with a metal stamp or engrave your initials. A finished casting should have no sharp edgesâfile them smooth.

lessons.title: Safety in Foundry Work
lessons.body: Foundry work can kill you if you ignore safety. Molten aluminum is 660Â°Câit will burn through flesh in a second. Never wear synthetic clothing (polyester, nylon) because it melts onto skin. Wear cotton or wool, leather boots, leather gloves, a leather apron, and a face shield. Tie back long hair. Work in a well-ventilated areaâoutdoors is best. Carbon monoxide from charcoal furnaces can kill you in a closed room. Keep a bucket of dry sand or a fire extinguisher nearby. Never use water on a metal fireâit explodes. For small spills, smother with dry sand. Before pouring, check your mold for moisture. Any dampness causes steam explosions. Preheat molds to at least 200Â°C. When melting, never look directly into the crucibleâuse a face shield. Use long-handled tongs to move the crucible. Never leave a hot crucible unattended. After pouring, let the mold cool completely before breaking it open. Hot metal can hide under sand. When grinding or sanding, wear a dust mask and safety glasses. Aluminum dust is flammableâkeep it away from sparks. In Africa, many foundries operate informally. Insist on basic safety: gloves, face shield, and a clear work area. Never work alone. Have a partner who can call for help. If you get a burn, cool it with clean water for 20 minutes and seek medical help. Prevention is cheaper than a hospital bill.

lessons.title: Project: Cast Aluminum Sculpture
lessons.body: For this project, you will cast a small aluminum sculpture using sand casting. Choose a simple shape: a turtle, a mask, or a geometric form. First, make a pattern from MDF. Carve or sand it to shape, leaving a 1.3% extra size for shrinkage. Seal it with shellac. Build a two-part flask from wood: a bottom (drag) and top (cope) that fit together with alignment pins. Place the pattern in the drag, pack foundry sand around it, and ram it firm. Flip, place the cope, and pack sand again. Remove the pattern, cut a sprue and riser. Melt about 1 kg of aluminum scrap in a clay-graphite crucible in a charcoal furnace. Preheat the mold to 250Â°C. Pour the molten aluminum into the sprue in one steady stream. Wait 15 minutes, then break the sand away. Cut off the sprue with a hacksaw. Grind and sand the surface: 80, 120, 220 grit. For a finish, heat the sculpture with a torch and rub with palm oilâit will turn black and glossy. Or leave it raw and polish with a wire brush. Sign your work. This project takes about 4 hours. If you don't have a furnace, you can use a local blacksmith's forge or a community foundry. In Africa, many artisans cast aluminum from recycled car parts. Your total cost: sand (free if you dig your own), clay (free), charcoal (about $2), and scrap aluminum (free or cheap). The skills you learn here can become a businessâcast aluminum sculptures sell in markets and galleries. Practice with simple shapes before attempting complex ones.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between sand casting and lost wax casting?
options: A) Sand casting uses wax patterns, lost wax uses sand
B) Sand casting uses a reusable pattern, lost wax uses a one-time wax pattern
C) Sand casting is only for iron, lost wax only for aluminum
D) Sand casting requires a kiln, lost wax does not
quiz.explanation: In sand casting the pattern is removed and reused; in lost wax the wax pattern is melted out and destroyed.

quiz.q: What is the typical shrinkage allowance for aluminum castings?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum shrinks about 1.3% when it solidifies and cools, so patterns must be made larger.

quiz.q: Why should you preheat a mold before pouring molten metal?
options: A) To make the metal flow faster
B) To prevent steam explosions from moisture
quiz.explanation: Any moisture in the mold turns to steam and can blow molten metal back at the caster.

quiz.q: What is the melting point of aluminum?
quiz.explanation: Aluminum melts at 660Â°C, which is achievable in a charcoal furnace.

quiz.q: Which material is best for a casting pattern?
quiz.explanation: MDF or pine is easy to carve, stable, and can be sealed with shellac.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a sprue in sand casting?
options: B) To pour molten metal into the mold
C) To hold the pattern in place
D) To add color to the metal
quiz.explanation: The sprue is the vertical channel through which molten metal enters the mold cavity.

quiz.q: What is a riser used for?
options: B) To allow gases to escape and feed shrinkage
C) To make the mold stronger
D) To cool the metal quickly
quiz.explanation: A riser acts as a reservoir of molten metal and allows gases to escape during pouring.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid pouring molten metal over concrete?
options: B) Concrete contains moisture that can cause explosions
C) Concrete makes the metal dirty
quiz.explanation: Concrete traps moisture, which turns to steam and can explosively spall when hit by molten metal.

quiz.q: What is the correct safety gear for foundry work?
options: B) Leather gloves, face shield, leather apron, cotton clothing
D) No gear needed for small pours
quiz.explanation: Leather and cotton protect against burns; synthetics melt onto skin.

quiz.q: How many coats of ceramic slurry are typical for lost wax shell building?
quiz.explanation: A strong ceramic shell usually requires 7 to 10 coats, drying between each.

quiz.q: What temperature is used to melt out wax from a ceramic shell?
quiz.explanation: Wax melts around 150Â°C; higher temperatures are for firing the shell.

quiz.q: What is dross in metal casting?
options: B) Impurities that float on molten metal
quiz.explanation: Dross is oxidized metal and other impurities that should be skimmed off before pouring.

quiz.q: Why is it dangerous to use a steel pot as a crucible for aluminum?
options: B) Steel melts at a lower temperature than aluminum
C) Steel conducts heat too slowly
quiz.explanation: Molten aluminum can dissolve steel, weakening the pot and contaminating the metal.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cleaning a raw casting?
options: B) Cut off the sprue and riser
quiz.explanation: The sprue and riser are excess metal that must be removed before finishing.

quiz.q: Which grit sandpaper is used first when finishing a casting?
quiz.explanation: Start with coarse 80 grit to remove rough spots, then progress to finer grits.

quiz.q: What is a common patina method using local African materials?
options: B) Heating and rubbing with palm oil
quiz.explanation: Heated metal rubbed with palm oil gives a black, glossy finish used by many African sculptors.

quiz.q: Why should you never work alone in a foundry?
options: B) You need someone to call for help in an emergency
quiz.explanation: If you are burned or injured, a partner can get help quickly.

quiz.q: What is the correct treatment for a molten metal burn?
options: B) Cool with clean water for 20 minutes and seek medical help
quiz.explanation: Cooling with water reduces tissue damage; medical help prevents infection.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a draft angle on a pattern?
options: A) To make the pattern look better
B) To allow easy removal from the sand mold
quiz.explanation: A slight taper (1-2 degrees) lets you pull the pattern out without breaking the mold.

quiz.q: What is parting dust used for?
options: B) To prevent sand from sticking to the pattern
quiz.explanation: Parting dust (talc or similar) creates a barrier so the pattern releases cleanly.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before breaking open a sand mold after pouring?
quiz.explanation: The metal needs to solidify and cool enough to handle; 10-15 minutes is typical for small castings.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of carbon monoxide in foundry work?
options: B) It is odorless and can kill in enclosed spaces
quiz.explanation: Carbon monoxide from charcoal furnaces is odorless and deadly; always work outdoors or ventilate well.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of charcoal for a small aluminum melt?
quiz.explanation: A small charcoal furnace uses about $2 worth of charcoal for a 1 kg aluminum melt.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good source of scrap aluminum for casting?
options: B) Car rims and window frames
quiz.explanation: Cans and foil are too thin and oxidize; cast scrap like rims gives better results.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a flask in sand casting?
options: A) To hold the sand mold
quiz.explanation: The flask (cope and drag) contains the packed sand that forms the mold.

quiz.q: Why is it important to ram the sand firmly?
options: A) To make the mold last longer
B) To prevent the mold from collapsing and to allow gas escape
D) To make the pattern easier to remove
quiz.explanation: Proper ramming gives strength but still allows gases to escape through the sand.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the lost wax process?
options: B) Carve the sculpture in wax
quiz.explanation: You start by creating the original wax model, which is then coated with ceramic.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of stuccoing in lost wax?
options: B) To build up the ceramic shell thickness
quiz.explanation: Stucco (fine sand) is applied between slurry coats to build a thick, strong shell.

quiz.q: Why should you wear a dust mask when sanding a casting?
options: A) To avoid inhaling metal and sand dust
B) To keep the metal clean
quiz.explanation: Metal and sand dust can damage lungs; a dust mask is essential.

quiz.q: What is a good way to sign your finished sculpture?
options: B) Stamp or engrave your initials
quiz.explanation: A metal stamp or engraving tool gives a permanent, professional signature.
